xep.header:
The /slap Command This specification defines the /slap command, by which a human user may slap another user around a bit with a large trout, in a manner faithful to the behaviour popularised by mIRC since 1995. It is offered as a tribute to mIRC and its author, and requires no new protocol whatsoever. &LEGALNOTICE; xxxx ProtoXEP Humorous None Editor
XMPP Core XMPP IM XEP-0245
slap &gdk;
1.0.0 2026-10-23 gdk First draft. Trout freshly caught.

section1.p: On the 28th of February, 1995, Khaled Mardam-Bey released the first public version of mIRC mIRC is a registered trademark of mIRC Co. Ltd. Its use in this document is purely referential and implies no endorsement by, or affiliation with, mIRC Co. Ltd. See <https://www.mirc.com/>., an IRC client for Windows. He started it because he found the IRC clients of that era hard to use or short on features, and wanted to see whether a client could be easy to use and fun at the same time. See the mIRC Personal FAQ <https://www.mirc.com/pfaq.html>. It could. mIRC went on to be downloaded more than 150 million times, grew entirely by word of mouth, and taught a generation of people what it meant to be "online" together, years before Jabber, the technology that became XMPP, was first announced in 1999. More than thirty years later, mIRC is still maintained by its original author.
Among the many things that generation learned from mIRC was a small piece of social ritual. Right-click a nickname in a channel, select "Slap!" from the popup menu, and the whole channel would read:

example.caption: The Slap, As Observed In The Wild

section1.example: * Mercutio slaps Tybalt around a bit with a large trout
section1.p: The slap did nothing. It changed no channel modes, kicked no one, and carried no protocol semantics of any kind: it was merely an action message. And yet it said a great deal: "you have made a minor, forgivable mistake", "I am fond of you", or simply "it is 3 AM and this channel is too quiet". The trout became, in effect, an emoji avant la lettre, with a payload of exactly one fish.

The XMPP community already recognises the value of IRC-originated conventions: &xep0245; documents the /me command, which many XMPP clients implement. This specification builds directly on that work. It standardises /slap for XMPP clients so that the slap behaves exactly as it does in mIRC, and it does so in order to say, on behalf of the XMPP community: thank you, mIRC, and thank you, Khaled, for three decades of paving the instant messaging way.
This specification addresses the following requirements:

ul.li: A user MUST be able to slap another user around a bit with a large trout.
The resulting slap MUST be indistinguishable from an mIRC slap, so that IRC veterans feel at home.
The slap MUST be received correctly by every client that implements &xep0245;, including clients that have never heard of this specification and those whose developers have never held a trout.
The specification MUST NOT introduce any new XML elements, namespaces, or service discovery features. Trout do not need to be discovered; they need only to be experienced.

di.dd: The user who initiates the slap.
The user who is slapped. Synonym: "the target".
A fish of the family Salmonidae, used here in a strictly metaphorical capacity. In this specification the trout is always large.

section2.p: A user invokes the command by typing, in the message input area of their client, the string "/slap" followed by a single space (U+0020) and the name of the slappee:

The command is case-sensitive, in the same way that &xep0245; matches only the exact string "/me ". The string "/SLAP" is not a command; it is shouting, and SHOULD be sent as ordinary text so that the room can see it.

The /slap command is processed entirely by the sending client. When the slapper's client detects that the text entered by the user begins with the string "/slap " (including the trailing space), it MUST NOT send that text as-is. Instead, it MUST compose a &xep0245; /me command whose verb phrase is exactly:
section2.example: slaps <target> around a bit with a large trout
section2.p: where <target> is replaced with the name of the slappee as determined below. The resulting text is then sent as the &BODY; of an otherwise ordinary message stanza. For example, if Mercutio is in a chatroom with the other young men of Verona and types "/slap Tybalt", his client sends:

example.caption: XMPP Stanza Resulting From a /slap Command

section2.example: <message from='verona@chat.shakespeare.lit/Mercutio' to='verona@chat.shakespeare.lit' type='groupchat'> <body>/me slaps Tybalt around a bit with a large trout</body> </message>
section2.p: The verb phrase MUST be reproduced character for character. In particular, a compliant implementation:

ul.li: MUST use the word "slaps"; not "hits", "whacks", "bonks", or "gently admonishes".
MUST include the words "around a bit". The slap is neither a single blow nor a sustained assault. It is around a bit.

MUST specify a trout. Substitution of any other fish is NOT RECOMMENDED. Substitution of a halibut is explicitly prohibited, on the grounds that halibut-based slapping is a separate prior art with its own, rather more famous, choreography. See "The Fish-Slapping Dance" (Monty Python's Flying Circus, 1972), in which Michael Palin slaps John Cleese with two small pilchards and is then felled by a much larger fish. Sources disagree on whether that fish is a halibut or a trout; this specification declines to adjudicate, and prohibits the halibut regardless. The sketch is sometimes cited as an inspiration for the mIRC slap.
MUST describe the trout as "large". Trout of other sizes are out of scope of this specification and MAY be addressed by future specifications, such as a hypothetical "/nudge with a small minnow" XEP.

section2.p: This construction is deliberate and mirrors mIRC: the "Slap!" entry in mIRC's default nickname list popup menu is a one-line script that issues an action command (the IRC equivalent of /me) with the same verb phrase. The mIRC help file uses this very line as an example of a nickname list popup: "Slap!:/me slaps $1 around a bit with a large trout", where $1 is the selected nickname. See <https://www.mirc.com/help/html/popups.html>. A /slap therefore has no protocol semantics beyond those of /me, just as the original slap had none beyond those of an IRC action.

mIRC itself has no built-in typed /slap command: its slap is always aimed at the single nickname selected in the nickname list. The typed form is a convention of user scripts and other clients, and this specification defines it in the spirit of the original. Scripts that define a typed /slap commonly use the mIRC identifier $$1, which refers to the first parameter and halts the script if that parameter is missing. A client:

ul.li: MUST use the first whitespace-delimited token after "/slap " as the target.
MUST ignore any further tokens. "/slap Tybalt with a halibut" results in Tybalt being slapped with a trout. Users cannot negotiate the fish.

MUST NOT send anything when no target is given (e.g., the user typed "/slap" or "/slap " on its own). The client MAY present a brief local hint, but MUST NOT slap the slapper by default. Self-slapping is a deliberate act and is covered below.

section2.p: Unlike IRC nicknames, the room nicknames used in &xep0045; may contain spaces (for example, "Friar Laurence"). Since such a nickname cannot be expressed as a single token, a client that offers nickname auto-completion MAY treat a completed occupant nickname as a single target, irrespective of embedded spaces. Clients SHOULD otherwise rely on the context menu for such targets. IRC nicknames cannot contain spaces, so mIRC never had to deal with this problem, and this specification addresses it with some reluctance.

The target string is reproduced as typed or selected by the slapper. The sending client MUST NOT resolve it to a JID, as this would leak information the slappee might wish to keep private, and also because nobody has ever been slapped by their JID.

Before composing the body, the sending client MUST remove any line break characters (U+000A, U+000D) from the target. A target that would make the resulting body span multiple lines is not a slap; it is an attempt to smuggle text past the reader inside a fish.

A user MAY slap themselves (e.g., "/slap Hamlet", typed by Hamlet). This is a legitimate expression of self-reproach, with considerable literary precedent See Hamlet, Act II, Scene 2: "O, what a rogue and peasant slave am I!", and MUST be processed in the same way as any other slap.

In mIRC, the slap is delivered not by typing but via the popup menu of the channel nickname list. Clients that present a list of chatroom occupants or contacts SHOULD offer, in the context menu of each entry, an item with the exact label:

The exclamation mark is part of the label and MUST NOT be omitted. Selecting the item MUST produce the same result as the user typing "/slap " followed by the nickname of the selected entry (in which case the full nickname, including any spaces, is the target).
Clients on touch devices MAY additionally trigger the item when the user performs a swiping motion over an occupant's entry, preferably in a flicking motion resembling the tail of a fish.
Nothing in this specification is specific to chatrooms. Because a slap is simply a &xep0245; /me command, it works unchanged in one-to-one chats, where it is sent in a message stanza of type 'chat':

example.caption: A Slap in a One-to-One Chat

section2.example: <message from='juliet@capulet.lit/balcony' to='romeo@montague.lit' type='chat'> <body>/me slaps Romeo around a bit with a large trout</body> </message>
section2.p: All the rules defined above apply here too. In particular, a bare "/slap" still sends nothing, even though there is only one plausible slappee. A slap in mIRC is always aimed at a named nickname, and the slapper is expected to name the slappee here too.

When a slap is triggered from the "Slap!" item in a contact list (see above), the client has to choose a name for the target. The slappee will read this name, so the client SHOULD use the nickname that the contact has published for themselves (see &xep0172;) when one is known, and SHOULD NOT use the private name under which the slapper has stored the contact in their roster. A roster name such as "Romeo (a Montague; hide from Father)" is not intended for Romeo's eyes, and a trout is no reason for him to see it.
A receiving client needs no knowledge of this specification. Because the slap arrives as a &xep0245; /me command, it will be presented accordingly, for example:
section2.example: * Mercutio slaps Tybalt around a bit with a large trout
section2.p: A receiving client that does implement this specification MAY recognise a /me command whose body matches the canonical verb phrase exactly and apply additional presentation, such as displaying a fish glyph (e.g., U+1F41F FISH) next to the message, or briefly shaking the slappee's entry in the occupant list. Such embellishments MUST NOT alter the text of the message, and MUST be possible for the user to disable. Readers are reminded that there is, regrettably, no dedicated trout character in Unicode; the generic FISH character is acceptable until the Unicode Consortium recognises its oversight.

A receiving client MUST NOT treat a slap as having any effect on room roles, affiliations, presence, or subscription state. Being slapped does not make one a moderator, although in the experience of the author it is correlated with it.

ul.li: A slap is a gesture of affection, mild rebuke, or both. It MUST NOT be construed as an endorsement of slapping anyone with anything outside of a chat client.
Clients SHOULD NOT offer a "slap everyone in the room" function. Mass trouting is a moderation problem, not a feature.
Room moderators retain all of their usual powers under &xep0045;, and are encouraged to use them against users who confuse frequency of slapping with quality of slapping.

Bots MAY respond to being slapped. A bot that responds by slapping the slapper back is RECOMMENDED to do so no more than once, to avoid infinite trout loops between bots (see Security Considerations).

section1.p: The canonical verb phrase is English and MUST NOT be translated. While it may seem inclusive to slap someone in their own language, any localisation would break the interoperability of the slap with thirty years of logs, quotes databases, and fond memories, and would also invite a protracted discussion about the regional availability of trout. Clients MAY localise the "Slap!" menu label for display purposes, but the transmitted text remains in English.

A client that presents messages aurally SHOULD present a slap in the manner prescribed for /me commands by &xep0245;, i.e., "Mercutio slaps Tybalt around a bit with a large trout". It MUST NOT play a wet slapping sound effect without the user having explicitly enabled such a feature, and SHOULD NOT offer such a feature in the first place.

Anyone may manually type the text "/me slaps Tybalt around a bit with a large trout". Such a message is indistinguishable from a slap generated by a /slap command, and receivers MUST NOT attempt to distinguish between them. This is by design: in mIRC, too, a hand-typed slap is a real slap. There is no such thing as a forged trout.

The security considerations of &xep0245; apply, in particular regarding the spoofing of presence notifications. A slap MUST NOT be presented in a way that could be confused with a system notification. "*** Tybalt has been slapped" is not a valid presentation.

Unrestricted slapping may be used to annoy (a "trout flood"). Clients SHOULD NOT provide automation for repeated slapping, and servers MAY apply their usual rate limits. No additional denial-of-service considerations arise, as a trout, however large, consists of a fixed number of octets.

Two bots configured to slap back whenever slapped will slap each other indefinitely. Implementers of such bots are referred to the business rules above, and to the general principle that any loop involving fish should be terminated as early as possible.
No trout are harmed in the implementation or use of this specification. The trout is entirely virtual, has no payload beyond its own description, and is released back into the stream after each use.

This document requires no interaction with &IANA;. Some consideration was given to establishing an IANA registry of approved fish, but it was decided that the list has exactly one entry, and that it is not open for registration.

This document requires no interaction with the ®ISTRAR;. It defines no namespaces, no service discovery features, and no XML schema. Implementations of this specification are therefore fully interoperable with every client that has ever implemented &xep0245;, which is, the author contends, the most successful reuse of a fish in the history of protocol design.

The author wishes to thank Khaled Mardam-Bey and mIRC Co. Ltd., for creating and maintaining mIRC for more than thirty years, and for showing an entire generation that chatting on the internet could be both easy and fun. Much of what instant messaging is today, in XMPP and elsewhere, stands on the shoulders of that work.

Thanks are also due to Jarkko Oikarinen, for creating IRC in 1988 and thereby giving the trout somewhere to swim; to Peter Saint-Andre, for &xep0245;, on which this specification depends entirely; to the Monty Python team, for the general principle of slapping people with fish; and to every IRC user who ever right-clicked a nickname at 3 AM and selected "Slap!".
